title: Hierarchical Abstract Tree for Cross-Document Retrieval Augmented Generation
claim: Prior tree-based retrieval degrades and becomes costly when scaling from one document to many; ours stays accurate and efficient.
layout: 3 panels: top scenario diagram, bottom-left line plot, bottom-right scatter with callouts
description: A wide rounded box at the top, panel (a), compares two retrieval scenarios as icon pipelines. The orange single-document row runs from a document to passage-level online indexing, to a database, to query search, and then to an augmented-context robot. The blue cross-document row runs from a multi-document corpus to corpus-level offline indexing, to cross-document query search, and then to a robot. Braces mark the offline and online stages. Below, panel (b) is a line chart of F1 against the number of documents (1 to 1000). Ψ-RAG, a blue line with stars, stays flat near 77. RAPTOR, a red line with diamonds, falls from 65 to 22. Panel (c) is a scatter of indexing time against F1. Ψ-RAG sits top-left, and colored text boxes label Graph-RAG and traditional Tree-RAG. The author name and a rule from the page header are visible at the top.
caption: (a) Two RAG application scenarios: single-document and cross-document retrieval. (b) Multi-hop QA performance w.r.t. the number of documents in the tree index. (c) Ψ-RAG has both efficient indexing and accurate multi-hop retrieval compared to structured RAG baselines, using 2Wiki as an example.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models with external knowledge, and tree-based RAG organizes documents into hierarchical indexes to support queries at multiple granularities. However, existing Tree-RAG methods designed for single-document retrieval face critical challenges in scaling to cross-document multi-hop questions: (1) poor distribution adaptability, where $k$-means clustering introduces noise due to rigid distribution assumptions; (2) structural isolation, as tree indexes lack explicit cross-document connections; and (3) coarse abstraction, which obscures fine-grained details. To address these limitations, we propose $Î¨$-RAG, a tree-RAG framework with two key components. First, a hierarchical abstract tree index built through an iterative "merging and collapse" process that adapts to data distributions without a priori assumption. Second, a multi-granular retrieval agent that intelligently interacts with the knowledge base with reorganized queries and an agent-powered hybrid retriever. $Î¨$-RAG supports diverse tasks from token-level question answering to document-level summarization. On cross-document multi-hop QA benchmarks, it outperforms RAPTOR by 25.9% and HippoRAG 2 by 7.4% in average F1 score. Code is available at https://github.com/Newiz430/Psi-RAG.
